findings.locator: Westminster Confession, chapter I §§2–3, complete list and Apocrypha exclusion
findings.document_finding: The confession lists its canonical Old Testament and excludes the books called Apocrypha from inspiration and canonical authority.
findings.qualification: This documents one Reformed confession, not all Protestant canons in every place or evidence the Catholic books first appeared at Trent.

findings.locator: Augustine, De doctrina christiana II.8.12–13, explicit list of canon
findings.document_finding: Augustine includes Tobit, Judith and two Maccabees within the list to which biblical authority is assigned.
findings.qualification: Augustine's witness establishes pre-Reformation reception, not identical canon practice among all ancient Christian churches.

findings.locator: Trent Session IV decree on sacred books and traditions (8 April 1546)
findings.document_finding: The council expressly receives written books, provides an enumerated canon and mentions unwritten apostolic traditions.
findings.qualification: Trent's decree cannot by itself establish unanimous second-century recognition of every listed book.

findings.locator: Jehovah's Witnesses' own John 1:1 exposition, origin of the Word and 'a god'
findings.document_finding: Their apologetic explicitly treats the Word as created and subordinate while denying that 'a god' entails polytheism.
findings.qualification: Do not ascribe to Witnesses a doctrine of three coequal divine persons or collapse their position into every historical form of Arianism.

findings.locator: John 1:1–18, prologue and the Word becoming flesh
findings.document_finding: John sets the Word's divine identity and distinction within the opening monotheistic account, later identifying the Word become flesh.
findings.qualification: This does not alone settle all grammatical debates over the article in Greek; historical exegesis remains separate.

findings.locator: Westminster I.6–10, sufficiency and supreme judge in controversies
findings.document_finding: The Reformed confession makes Scripture's teaching sufficient and the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture the ultimate judge in religious disputes.
findings.qualification: This does not mean all historical Protestants deny any value to creeds, synods or received interpretations.

findings.locator: Westminster XXXI.3–4, fallibility of post-apostolic synods and councils
findings.document_finding: Westminster holds that later synods or councils may err and must not be made rules of faith apart from Scripture.
findings.qualification: That is a specific Reformed challenge to irreformable ecclesial definitions, not wholesale rejection of Church deliberation.

findings.locator: Westminster XXVII.4, two gospel sacraments
findings.document_finding: The confession expressly identifies Baptism and the Lord's Supper as the only two sacraments instituted by Christ in the gospel.
findings.qualification: Its 'signs and seals' account must not be caricatured as teaching that sacraments communicate no grace.

findings.locator: Westminster XXIV.5–6, adultery and irremediable wilful desertion
findings.document_finding: The confession permits divorce and subsequent marriage for adultery and states an additional dissolution ground for incurable desertion.
findings.qualification: It also requires a public orderly proceeding; 'divorce on personal whim' is not its stated position.

findings.locator: Ephesians 5:21–33, reciprocal Christian duties and Christ–Church union
findings.document_finding: The passage begins its marriage instructions with mutual subordination in reverence for Christ and commands husbands to love sacrificially.
findings.qualification: It does not supply a standalone civil marriage-law procedure or license coercion and abuse.

findings.locator: Westminster XXIX.5–7, unchanged elements and real spiritual reception
findings.document_finding: Westminster rejects substantial conversion of bread and wine while teaching spiritually real reception of Christ by faith.
findings.qualification: It is not accurate to equate its Eucharistic account with a doctrine of mere social symbolism.

findings.locator: Westminster XXIX.1–2, remembrance and anti-propitiatory argument
findings.document_finding: The confession expressly calls the Catholic propitiatory Mass contrary to Christ's sole saving sacrifice while presenting the Supper as communion.
findings.qualification: Represent the vigorous actual opponent argument, not a softened invention that the Reformed merely dislike Catholic ceremonies.

findings.locator: Westminster XXI.2, divine worship and rejection of saint invocation
findings.document_finding: The confession requires religious worship to be directed to the Trinity alone and excludes angels and saints as recipients.
findings.qualification: Catholic distinction of adoration and honour must answer the specific Reformed objection without pretending all honour is worship.

findings.locator: Westminster XXI.2, prohibition of prayer to saints
findings.document_finding: Westminster expressly excludes saints and angels from recipients of religious worship and prayer.
findings.qualification: This is a direct confessional challenge to saintly intercession, not a proof that historical Catholics attribute divinity to saints.

findings.locator: Westminster XXI.1, regulated worship and visible representation
findings.document_finding: The Reformed account excludes worship according to human invention and rejects visible representation as a worship method.
findings.qualification: The Catholic distinction between idolatry and sacred images needs its own Trent and scriptural analysis.

findings.locator: Westminster XI.1–2, imputed righteousness and saving faith
findings.document_finding: The confession makes justification a free act of divine acceptance on account of Christ rather than infusion as its formal ground.
findings.qualification: The same confession distinguishes justification from sanctification; it does not declare Christian obedience unnecessary.

findings.locator: Lumen gentium §§14–16 on Church necessity and different persons' relationship to salvation
findings.document_finding: The constitution affirms the Church's necessity while recognising conditions for salvation where knowledge of the Gospel is non-culpably absent.
findings.qualification: These possibilities cannot be rephrased as a claim that every religion provides its own independent saviour.

findings.locator: Dominus Iesus §20 on necessary Church and universal salvific will
findings.document_finding: The declaration holds together the possibility of salvation for all in Christ and the necessary relation to the Church.
findings.qualification: It does not describe all religious traditions as equal independent means to salvation.

findings.locator: Westminster XXXII.1, immediate state of the soul after death
findings.document_finding: The confession sends the righteous to heaven and the wicked to hell, and says Scripture acknowledges no third place for separated souls.
findings.qualification: This is a clear Reformed rejection of purgatory; it must be tested against the Catholic canon and final purification, not against a caricature of paid release.

findings.locator: Westminster III.1, III.3 and III.7; XVIII, sin, election and assurance
findings.document_finding: The confession denies God authors sin yet describes both foreordination to death and passing by, with condemnation for sin.
findings.qualification: A strong Catholic criticism must preserve the confession's denial that God is the author of evil.

findings.locator: Catechism §1037: no predestination to hell
findings.document_finding: The Catechism expressly denies divine predestination of anyone to hell and speaks of a wilful turning away and persistence to death.
findings.qualification: The formulation does not resolve all scholastic disagreements over efficacious grace and the order of foreknowledge.

findings.locator: Nostra aetate §4, the Church's link to Israel and rejection of collective guilt
findings.document_finding: The declaration affirms the Jewish roots of the Church and expressly rejects imputing Christ's death indiscriminately to present Jews.
findings.qualification: It does not teach that Christian confession of Jesus as Messiah is interchangeable with the beliefs of every Jewish community.

findings.locator: Romans 11:1–2, 17–24, 28–29, God's irrevocable calling and grafting
findings.document_finding: Paul denies God has rejected Israel and warns Gentile Christians against arrogant boasting, while speaking of faith and grafting into the olive tree.
findings.qualification: This is not a conclusion that rabbinic Judaism and Christianity have identical doctrines or independently equivalent soteriologies.

findings.locator: Qur'an 4:157, death and crucifixion of Jesus
findings.document_finding: The Qur'anic passage denies that Jesus' opponents killed or crucified him as Christianity teaches.
findings.qualification: The interpretation of the wider Qur'anic account varies; this verse alone does not validate assertions about its literary source.

findings.locator: Abu Dhabi 4 February 2019 Declaration, paragraph beginning 'Freedom is a right'
findings.document_finding: The signed text expressly states that diversity of religions alongside other forms of diversity is willed by God in wisdom.
findings.qualification: The possible permissive-will reading is an interpretive response and should never be substituted for the wording actually signed.

findings.locator: Dominus Iesus §§5–7 and 13–15 on singularity of Christ's revelation and mediation
findings.document_finding: Dominus Iesus rejects relativising the definitive revelation and unique salvific mediation of Christ.
findings.qualification: This doctrinal baseline does not show that all peace-oriented dialogue is indifferentism.
